bibl.title: Frequency selectivity of echo responses in the mouse primary auditory cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: echo responses - activity at the anticipated time after a rhythmic tone train ends - in layer 2/3 neurons of mouse A1
span.quote: In the primary auditory cortex (A1), neuronal ensembles are activated relative to anticipated sound events following rhythmic stimulation, but whether the echo responses of the neurons are related to their frequency selectivity remains unknown.

span.label: whether a neuron's echo response depends on which frequency was used, that is on its own frequency tuning
span.quote: Although the prediction correlated neural signals have already been observed in multiple sensory regions in different mammals, the stimulus type for the preferentially evoked echo responses is unclear. Specifically, whether the echo responses of the neurons in the auditory cortex are related to their frequency selectivity remains unknown.

span.label: shows echo responses occur preferentially at each neuron's best frequency, in both anaesthetised and awake mice, while their spatial arrangement stays locally heterogeneous
span.quote: After testing with a range of frequencies, we found that these echo responses occurred preferentially close to the best frequencies of the neurons.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We confirmed the presence of echo responses in a subgroup of mouse Layer 2/3 A1 neurons following a train of rhythmic pure tone stimulation.

span.label: echo responses (omitted stimulus-evoked responses) in primary auditory cortex
span.quote: Specifically, whether the echo responses of the neurons in the auditory cortex are related to their frequency selectivity remains unknown.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Therefore, we used in vivo two-photon Ca 2+ imaging to record the neuronal activities in the mouse A1 to elucidate the relationship between their echo responses and frequency selectivity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: We propose that, there is scale-free topology in the cortical network, which contains hub neurons in L2/3 and many low-degree loops with different lengths in L5

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: After learning through a train of rhythmic sensory stimulation, a loop with certain length is selected to match the input rhythm. Finally, the network is able to generate echo responses with the same rhythm.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: These low-degree loops enable the neural system to follow the external input rhythm, while hub neurons can trigger synchronization in the whole network.

span.label: a proposed scale-free cortical topology: low-degree L5 loops of differing length follow the input rhythm, one loop is selected to match it, and L2/3 hub neurons synchronise the network
span.quote: We propose that, there is scale-free topology in the cortical network, which contains hub neurons in L2/3 and many low-degree loops with different lengths in L5 (Fig. 5 ; modified from the previous study 5 ). These low-degree loops enable the neural system to follow the external input rhythm, while hub neurons can trigger synchronization in the whole network. During learning, the connectivity from the L5 loops to the L2/3 hubs is highly strengthened, which allows the signals to flow across the entire network. After learning through a train of rhythmic sensory stimulation, a loop with certain length is selected to match the input rhythm. Finally, the network is able to generate echo responses with the same rhythm.

span.label: the echo is treated as an intrinsic property of cortical circuits responding to the absence of an expected sound, not as a residue of the sound response
span.quote: Therefore, it implies that echo response is an intrinsic property of cortical circuits in response to the absence of an expected sound, and echo response may reflect a distinct neural process in comparison to sound-evoked responses.

span.label: longer latency and lower amplitude of echoes attributed to across-neuron variation in estimating the input rhythm
span.quote: Those differences could be attributed to a variation in neurons for the estimation of the input rhythm, and it thus leads to a longer latency and a lower amplitude of the echo responses on average.

span.label: the imaged region is identified as A1 by its thalamic connectivity, using retrograde tracer to MGBv, rather than by the response property under study
span.quote: To verify that the imaged cortical regions were located in the A1, we used the criterion 44 , 45 that the ventral part of the lateral medial geniculate body (MGBv) is connecting with A1.

span.label: indicator sensitivity is decisive because most cortical neurons fire only one or two spikes to a sound, so a dye that misses single spikes misses the population
span.quote: The sensitivity plays the most important role in studying the organization of the A1, because most of cortical neurons respond with only one or two spikes to sound stimulation

span.label: predictive coding framing: the brain fits an internal model and minimises the discrepancy between predicted and actual input
span.quote: Theoretically, predictive coding suggests that the brain is constantly making efforts to ‘fit’ internal models in perceiving through inferring the incoming sensory input. The discrepancies between the actual sensory data and the predicted sensory data (‘error’) are used to refine the model in an iterative process until the model optimized

span.label: Evidence in the auditory field is still insufficient to decide whether prediction and error neurons occupy separate cortical layers.
span.quote: However, evidences by far are still deficient in the auditory field in accordance with the notion that prediction and error neurons reside separately in distinct cortical layers 56 , which shall be studied further.

span.label: How anaesthesia affects mouse A1 neurons remains largely unknown, so the anaesthetised results carry that uncertainty.
span.quote: However, the precise effects of anesthesia on A1 neurons of mouse are still largely unknown and hence need further investigation.

span.label: The behavioural relevance of the heterogeneous echo-response organisation was not established.
span.quote: However, the underlying mechanisms of contribution to behavior are still largely unknown and warrant investigation in future studies.

span.label: the precise effects of anaesthesia on mouse A1 neurons are still largely unknown, and the awake replication is the only guard
span.quote: However, the precise effects of anesthesia on A1 neurons of mouse are still largely unknown and hence need further investigation.

span.label: no behavioural measure, so the contribution of these responses to behaviour is untested
span.quote: However, the underlying mechanisms of contribution to behavior are still largely unknown and warrant investigation in future studies.

span.quote: However, evidences by far are still deficient in the auditory field in accordance with the notion that prediction and error neurons reside separately in distinct cortical layers 56 , which shall be studied further.

span.label: male mice only, with no analysis by sex
span.quote: C57BL/6J mice (male, 2–3 months old) were supplied by the Laboratory Animal Center of the Third Military Medical University.

span.quote: To improve visibility here, the frequency tuning curves were fitted by Gaussian function.

span.quote: The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

span.label: overall tuning across echo neurons was broad at the sound level used, which weakens the frequency-specificity claim it is set against
span.quote: Although the overall tuning for sound-evoked responses across all of the echo neurons (Fig. 3c ) was relatively broad given the sound level used here, the echo responses in most of the neurons occurred at the preferred frequencies.

span.label: predictive coding and iterative error minimisation, imported as the interpretive frame for an omitted-stimulus response
span.quote: Theoretically, predictive coding suggests that the brain is constantly making efforts to ‘fit’ internal models in perceiving through inferring the incoming sensory input. The discrepancies between the actual sensory data and the predicted sensory data (‘error’) are used to refine the model in an iterative process until the model optimized

span.label: scale-free topology and hub nodes, imported as the circuit explanation for rhythm following
span.quote: We propose that, there is scale-free topology in the cortical network, which contains hub neurons in L2/3 and many low-degree loops with different lengths in L5 (Fig. 5 ; modified from the previous study 5 ). These low-degree loops enable the neural system to follow the external input rhythm, while hub neurons can trigger synchronization in the whole network. During learning, the connectivity from the L5 loops to the L2/3 hubs is highly strengthened, which allows the signals to flow across the entire network. After learning through a train of rhythmic sensory stimulation, a loop with certain length is selected to match the input rhythm. Finally, the network is able to generate echo responses with the same rhythm.

span.label: echo response here means a response at the anticipated time AFTER the sound stops - it has nothing to do with acoustic echoes; the corpus also contains echo suppression in Muniak2014, where the echo is a real reflected sound
span.quote: These studies have shown that repetitive stimulation at a regular inter-stimulus interval (ISI) can result in neuronal activity at the anticipated time interval after stimulation, a phenomenon known as “omitted stimulus-evoked responses” or “echo responses

span.label: tonotopic organization is scale-dependent in this paper: present at about 1 mm, absent below 200 microns, so the same claim is true or false depending on the scale at which it is asserted
span.quote: The precise tonotopic organization in auditory cortex is a long debated issue 20 , 21 , 26 and remains unresolved. On the macroscopic scale level (~1 mm), the tonotopic map in the A1 arises from MGBv. However, the frequency selectivity of neighboring neurons can be very different, and no reliable tonotopic organization could be observed over spatial scales of <200 µm

span.label: A1 is identified by thalamic connectivity from MGBv, not by the frequency responses being studied - an external criterion, as in Humphries2010's core/belt boundary
span.quote: To verify that the imaged cortical regions were located in the A1, we used the criterion 44 , 45 that the ventral part of the lateral medial geniculate body (MGBv) is connecting with A1.

span.label: best frequency here is read off a Gaussian fit to 11 log-spaced frequencies between 2 and 40 kHz, each repeated 20 times
span.quote: To test the frequency tuning properties of single neurons, 11 frequencies logarithmically spaced in the range of 2–40 kHz were used in our experiment. Every frequency of stimulation was repeated 20 times, with the inter-stimulus interval (ISI) of 2 s.

span.label: local heterogeneity - neighbouring neurons with very different tuning - is presented as embedded within the global tonotopic order rather than as its refutation
span.quote: Therefore, these studies demonstrate that a rough tonotopic organization emerges at large scales, but local heterogeneity emerges at fine scales (<250 μm) and is embedded in the global tonotopic order

span.label: extends → the authors' earlier report of predictive sound information in A1 using broadband noise stimulation (ref. 5)
span.quote: This is consistent with the representations of predictive sound information in the A1 reported in a previous study that used broadband noise stimulation 5 .

span.label: builds-on → the network model of Mi et al. (ref. 51) for rhythmic synchronous firing
span.quote: For the possible mechanisms of how echo responses arise, a model proposed by Mi et al . 51 matches our previous 5 and current results.

span.label: extends → the earlier report of echo responses to broadband noise, by showing the effect is frequency-specific
span.quote: After the end of the rhythmic tone stimulation, these neurons exhibited 1–5 additional responses at the expected times for the same ISI (Fig. 2b , red), which is consistent with the neuronal echo response that has been described recently

span.label: supports → Mi et al's network model of rhythmic synchronous firing
span.quote: We propose that, there is scale-free topology in the cortical network, which contains hub neurons in L2/3 and many low-degree loops with different lengths in L5 (Fig. 5 ; modified from the previous study 5 ). These low-degree loops enable the neural system to follow the external input rhythm, while hub neurons can trigger synchronization in the whole network. During learning, the connectivity from the L5 loops to the L2/3 hubs is highly strengthened, which allows the signals to flow across the entire network. After learning through a train of rhythmic sensory stimulation, a loop with certain length is selected to match the input rhythm. Finally, the network is able to generate echo responses with the same rhythm.

span.label: supports → reports of local functional heterogeneity in A1 below 200 microns
span.quote: Therefore, these studies demonstrate that a rough tonotopic organization emerges at large scales, but local heterogeneity emerges at fine scales (<250 μm) and is embedded in the global tonotopic order

span.label: qualifies → studies of tonotopic organisation conducted under anaesthesia
span.quote: Early studies have shown that tonal selectivity in cats 59 and response variability in rats 60 were increased under anesthesia, suggesting anesthetics would alter tonotopic map to be stricter and more regular.

span.label: partially-supports → predictive coding as an account of cortical function
span.quote: Our studies based on unexpectedly omitted stimuli can give support for the prospective and predictive property of the expectancy outcomes, which would suggest the echo response as possibly the signature finding of predictive coding, as it is even able to be observed when sensory input is absent.

span.quote: When comparing the sound response with the echo response, we found the average amplitude of the sound responses (0.083 ± 0.002 Δf/f) for all of the imaged neurons in L2/3 was significantly higher than that of the echo responses (0.055 ± 0.003 Δf/f, n = 777 neurons from 8 mice, P < 0.001; Fig. 2e ), and the latency of the sound responses (0.083 ± 0.001 s) was significantly shorter than that of the echo responses (0.237 ± 0.024 s, n = 777 neurons from 8 mice, P < 0.001; Fig. 2f ).

span.quote: In addition, we performed a post hoc histological experiment with a retrograde neuronal tracer, CTB, which was injected into the imaged area (Fig. 1d ) and we found retrogradely-labeled cortical projecting neurons mainly located in the ventral part of the lateral medial geniculate body (MGBv) (Fig. 1e ), confirming that the recorded cortical site was located on the A1.

span.quote: In brief, we applied isoflurane at the level of 1–2% in pure oxygen for anesthesia and placed the animals onto a heating plate at a temperate of 37.5–38 °C. After local anesthesia with lidocaine, we removed the skin and muscle over the A1. Then the skull was glued with a customized plastic chamber using cyanoacrylic glue (UHU) and a ~2 × 2 mm small craniotomy was made centered at 2.5 mm posterior to bregma and 4.5 mm lateral to midline. After that, we reduced the isoflurane level to 0.4–0.8% and transferred the animal to the imaging system.
